extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, DHS adjudicators, policymakers, and public commenters on the proposed public charge rule
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for adjudicating the public-charge ground of inadmissibility, specifying which public benefits count, how to treat monetizable vs non-monetizable benefits, numeric/value and duration thresholds, counting rules, and related procedural considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider cash and non-cash public benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to consider cash benefits and non-cash public benefits in the public charge inadmissibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS believes consideration of cash and non-cash benefit receipt represents an appropriately comprehensive and also readily administrable application of the public charge ground of inadmissibility. Certain non-cash benefits, like cash benefits, provide assistance to those who are not self-sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipt alone is not determinative; focus on self-sufficiency and totality of circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: While an alien’s receipt of one or more of these benefits alone would not establish that he or she is likely at any time in the future to become a public charge, case law strongly suggests that an alien’s self-sufficiency plays a critical role in the outcome of a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ultimate inquiry is whether the alien is likely, in the totality of the circumstances, to become a public charge (i.e., to receive designated public benefits above applicable threshold(s), in dollar value or duration). Receipt of benefits is one factor among others; DHS recognizes dependence is a continuum of degree and duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective vs. retrospective treatment depending on application type
rubrics_metrics.description: For admissibility and adjustment of status purposes, receipt of such benefits is determined on a prospective basis (likely at any time to receive benefits above proposed thresholds). For extension of stay and change of status applicants, the determination regarding receipt above the proposed threshold is based on whether an alien has received since obtaining the nonimmigrant status in question, is receiving, or is likely at any time to receive benefits above the proposed threshold(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators should apply different temporal standards depending on the form of application: prospective for admissions/adjustments, partly historical for extensions/changes tied to the period since obtaining the nonimmigrant status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the 'primarily dependent' (50%) standard as required
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS does not believe section 212(a)(4) requires an alien to be 'primarily' (50 percent or more) dependent on the government or to rely only on cash assistance to be considered a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS views the statutory term 'public charge' as ambiguous about degree/type of assistance; it is permissible and reasonable to propose alternative approaches (e.g., percentage-of-FPG and duration thresholds) rather than the historic 50% income dependence model.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15 percent of Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) threshold for monetizable benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Receipt of monetizable public benefits whose cumulative value exceeds 15 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) for a household of one within any period of 12 consecutive months is a proposed trigger for being considered a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculation: compare cumulative monetizable benefit value over any 12 consecutive months to 15% of the per-month average FPG for those months. Example: 15% of FPG equals $1,821 for a household of one for Jan–Dec 2018 (FPG $12,140 × 0.15). For 12-month periods spanning two calendar years, compute using the applicable monthly FPGs and sum (example provided for Apr 2017–Mar 2018). For likely future receipt, DHS would use the FPG in effect on the date of adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use FPG as baseline for monetizable threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to use the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) as the baseline for the percentage-of-income (monetizable) standard because the guidelines are authoritative and transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: FPG is a simplified version of Census poverty thresholds, updated annually based on CPI-U; other federal programs use the poverty guidelines and percentage multiples thereof as eligibility standards (e.g., 125% or 185%). DHS uses FPG in other immigration contexts (e.g., affidavit of support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of monetizable benefits below the 15% threshold as evidence in totality
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS seeks comment on whether receipt of designated monetizable public benefits at or below the 15 percent threshold should be considered as evidence in the totality of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example alternatives: adjudicators could assign some weight to past/current receipt equal to 10% of FPG and less weight to receipt equal to 5% of FPG. DHS solicits views and data on whether the proposed 15% is appropriate, too low, or too high, or whether another monetizable basis (other than % of FPG or duration) is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12-month standard for non-monetizable benefits within 36 months
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to consider certain non-monetizable public benefits (e.g., Medicaid) if received for more than 12 cumulative months during a 36-month period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because DHS lacks an easily administrable standard to monetize some non-cash benefits, duration of receipt is used as a proxy for reliance: >12 cumulative months in any 36-month window indicates lack of self-sufficiency. Rationale includes precedent for considering duration (e.g., long-term institutionalization) and state/federal time limits intended to promote self-sufficiency (e.g., TANF 60-month limit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting method for non-monetizable benefits (overlap and multiple benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: When tallying non-monetizable benefits for the cumulative-months standard, multiple non-monetizable benefits received in the same month are counted additively, and months need not be consecutive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: receipt of Medicaid for 9 months plus public housing for 6 months within the same 36-month period equals 15 months of non-monetizable benefit receipt—counts regardless of overlap, consecutiveness, or timing within the 36 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination rule: reduced duration threshold when monetizable and non-monetizable benefits are both received
rubrics_metrics.description: If an alien receives monetizable benefits equal to or below the 15 percent of FPG threshold together with one or more non-monetizable public benefits, DHS proposes reducing the non-monetizable duration threshold from 12 months to 9 months in a 36-month period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to address circumstances where the combination of both types of benefits indicates questionable self-sufficiency even though neither alone crosses its standalone threshold. Counting: two different non-monetizable benefits in one month counts as two months; combinations that amount to 9 aggregate months in 36 months would meet the combination standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetizable public benefit: Supplemental Security Income (SSI)
rubrics_metrics.description: SSI is treated as a monetizable public benefit that provides monthly income payments to ensure a minimum level of income for the disabled, blind, or aged with limited income and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SSI is financed by general revenues and represented significant federal expenditures (~$54.7B in FY2017). Receipt of SSI would be included in the monetizable benefits cumulative-value calculation under the 15% of FPG standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetizable public benefit: Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF)
rubrics_metrics.description: TANF is treated as a monetizable public benefit providing monthly income assistance to low-income families intended to foster self-sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TANF cash assistance expenditures were significant (~$4.4B FY2016). Receipt of TANF cash assistance would be included in the monetizable benefits cumulative-value calculation under the 15% of FPG standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetizable public benefit: General Assistance (cash benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: State/local 'General Assistance' programs that provide cash or money instruments for income maintenance qualify as cash public benefits under this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General Assistance aids needy individuals or families who do not qualify for major programs or whose benefits are insufficient. If the aid is cash (not in-kind vouchers) and intended for income maintenance, it qualifies as a monetizable/cash public benefit for the 15% calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetizable public benefit: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)
rubrics_metrics.description: SNAP is included as a non-cash, monetizable public benefit because benefits are delivered as monthly dollar amounts on EBT cards and indicate lack of self-sufficiency for basic food needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SNAP is among the largest federal expenditures for low-income people. The dollar value credited monthly to an EBT card is monetizable and counts toward the 15% of FPG cumulative-value calculation. Disaster SNAP is excluded (different legal authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetizable public benefits: Housing programs (Section 8 vouchers, project-based rental assistance, Public Housing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain high-expenditure housing-related benefits (Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers, Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance, and Public Housing) are proposed to be considered as monetizable public benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These programs provide shelter-related assistance (below-market rent or subsidies) and impose significant federal expense; although noncitizen participation is relatively low, DHS proposes to include them as part of public charge determinations because they relate to a basic living need (shelter) and federal expenditures are significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of administrable method to monetize some non-cash benefits; use duration proxy
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS lacks an easily administrable standard for monetizing some non-cash benefits and therefore proposes duration-based thresholds for certain non-monetizable benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because some non-cash benefits cannot be readily monetized for adjudication, DHS uses cumulative-months of receipt over a 36-month period (e.g., >12 months) as a reasonable proxy for reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation for public comments on thresholds, monetization approaches, and timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS seeks public comments on whether the proposed thresholds (15% FPG for monetizable benefits, 12 months for non-monetizable benefits, 9 months combination rule), alternatives for monetizing benefits, and timeframes are appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS specifically requests data or views on whether thresholds are appropriate, too low, or too high; whether alternative bases (not % of FPG or duration) exist; whether benefits below thresholds should be given limited weight in totality; and any studies supporting alternative durations or monetization methods.
